speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

With respect to the Combines Investigation Act itself, which, in my opinion, is one of the most important pieces of legislation in Canada, I may say that it has been revised periodically and probably should be revised again in the light of developments over the past few years. I should like to have the minister, if he would, give the committee an indication of the scope of the operations of the administrators of these two groups which are established under that act, particularly in the light of an article which appeared in the Financial Post about the middle of June of this year, I believe it was, which indicated that there may be a change in view on the part of the officials administering the act or the government concerning the rules applying to mergers, combines, monopolies and other similar organizations.
I wonder whether the minister could indicate, in a general way at first, the effect of the operations of the act, and especially whether there is any change in attitude of the administrators or the minister as indicated in the article which appeared in the Financial Post.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think I must say, Mr. Chairman, that the article was one which reflected the views and opinions of the writer, not of

Supply-Justice
the minister or of the department. I have said, I think in the house since taking office and elsewhere, that we are making a study of the general scheme of the combines legislation as it is in effect in Canada today. My hon. friend will appreciate that there have been alterations to similar legislation in other countries, notably in the United Kingdom in recent years. I think it behooves any government, especially one taking office for the first time after a good many years, to make a study of matters of this kind and especially of matters of this kind which are so inextricably interrelated with questions of economic policy. It is in that sense I have, on the various occasions when I have spoken, indicated that we are making a study of the combines legislation, and of its impact on Canadian economic interests. I used the words "economic interests" as applied to the nation and not as applied to particular individuals.
In the case of this particular inquiry into yeast, the commission found, as I recall, that there was no evidence of an offence. There had been, in fact, a merger, but it was not a merger which brought the companies concerned within the terms of the legislation which requires evidence of detriment to the public. In effect, they found that the company, while effecting a merger which did give an increased measure of control, that measure of control had not proceeded to the point where it was likely to be detrimental to the public. It was inherent in their findings, if it was not explicit, that any further activities of this sort, any further mergers or acquisition of other companies in this field would, however, be very likely to bring the whole situation within the territory where there might well be an offence under the act.
It is in that light we are studying it. We Mr- Howard: If I understood the minister are making particular studies, of course, of correctly with respect to that last part of particular aspects of it, such as those which	comment-his comments related to the
arise under section 34 and under section 412-Teast industry, did they?
of the Criminal code which present particular problems within the over-all study to which I have referred. Having said that, I come back to the statement I made at the beginning. I can take no responsibility for the views expressed in the article in the Financial Post.

If I could elaborate a bit there, I might say that from what I can recall from reading this particular article, it arose out of a report of the restrictive trade practices commission on yeast. Apparently there was an opinion expressed in that report-I am not trying to interpret the report but merely to relate my remembrance of it- relating to the detriment, if any, to the general public of this particular merger in the yeast industry, or the acquisition of one company by another. In earlier reports of the commission dealing with similar types of mergers there was no reference to the degree of effect that it would have on the general public, so this report was taken to be a departure from the approach in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As I recall there was no departure in this report from what has been the practice in the past. The act itself now, and for many years, has authorized the procedure under which, if the commission itself is of the opinion that there is no evidence of an offence or nothing in the subject that they have investigated which warrants further action, then they may so report and recommend to the minister that no further action be taken; that provision has been in the act for some time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
If there were any further acquisitions or mergers by this company, then it might come within the ambit of the legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think to put it correctly, that would represent circumstances warranting a further investigation to establish whether or not, in fact, that further acquisition did not constitute an offence under the act.

Of course, we might get into the question of whether or not monopolies, by themselves, are detrimental, and what action can be taken with respect to them. From what I can recall of this yeast merger, Standard Brands, I believe it was, was the large company which acquired the control or bought out some other company. This, in effect, gave Standard Brands 100 per cent control over the production of one type of yeast and 85 per cent or 80 per cent control over the production of other types of yeast in Canada. Only one other company was left in the yeast producing business, and that was confined to the province of Quebec. In effect, therefore, the acquisition by Standard Brands Limited of this other company placed them in a position of having a virtual monopoly in the production, distribution and sale of yeast in Canada, with the exception of the province of Quebec.
If that situation is correctly stated or if a similar situation arose, in what position is that monopoly with respect to the legislation? Would these facts, by themselves, constitute an offence?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In the case of a merger the requirements of the act under section 2 are that the merger, trust or monopoly has operated or is likely to operate to the detriment or against the interests of the public, whether consumers, producers or others. The commission, in this case, found that the facts disclosed on the inquiry led to certain conclusions.
Firstly, that no monopolistic intent was shown on the part of Standard Brands and, secondly, that the price paid by Standard Brands for Best Yeast was not shown to be excessive, nor was Best Yeast pressured to sell but, on the contrary, the approach came from Best Yeast. As I recall it, Best Yeast was in a strong financial position. They made the approach. They said: if you will pay us a reasonable price we would rather sell out than continue in operation.
Thirdly, the reasons given by Standard Brands for the acquisition, that is to provide needed expansion of capacity and reduce freight costs by having better located plants, appear to be sound business reasons.
I might elaborate on that a little. If you have a business or an enterprise, such as many are in Canada, where very large sums of capital are required to get into that business, then anything whereby competition is lessened, or competitors are acquired, naturally tends to place the person acquiring it in a very powerful monopolistic position. But where you have a form of activity with regard to which no great sums of capital are required in order to be able to enter, and where the channels of distribution are relatively open and free so that entering into that business is, on the face of it, not terribly difficult, the mere acquisition by one company of a competitor does not, in that field, place the company in a very powerful position. That is what the commission had in mind in referring to this factor.
They further found that the slight increase in the price of Best Yeast to the jobber which apparently resulted from the merger may have been accompanied by an improvement in quality and cannot be said to involve detriment to the public.
On the basis of these factors the commission found there was no creation of a monopoly to the detriment of the public, but they did, as I say, warn that this merger has considerably narrowed both existing competition and the opportunity for competition in the industry, and that it has strengthened what may be called Standard Brands monopoly position.
I would sum up as follows: In the result, the commission was not convinced that the public interest had been so affected as to
Supply-J ustice
justify it recommending action to dissolve the merger. Its concern at the reduction in competition and the possibility of long term injury arising from the near monopoly position created led it, however, to express the opinion that Standard Brands should not be permitted to acquire either Lallemand's, of which there was no immediate suggestion, or any new competitor that might enter the present field.
It amounts to a finding that there was no evidence sufficient to warrant a finding of a monopoly operating against the interest of the public, but there was evidence which warranted the commission keeping a close eye on the situation and issuing a warning that further activities along these lines would immediately result in further investigation.

Following along the same line, and referring to the question of the press in Canada, especially the daily press, we have no particular monopoly except in specific towns and, in a sense, these monopolies make sense because a competitor could not make a go of it with any reasonable financial chance. But there has been a considerable growth of newspaper chains in this country which is tending toward a monopoly and there has also been the development of a co-operative press organization, the Canadian Press, which in effect means that a member of the Canadian Press is in a perfect position in competition with anyone who may intend to get into the business but who does not belong to the Canadian Press, and according to the Canadian Press regulations as they are presently set up it is almost impossible for a new enterprise to get going in that field and to be accepted by the Canadian Press.
With regard to this question of the development of chains in the newspaper area and the control of this system of sending press information across the country, is the combines investigation branch watching developments in this particular field at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, I think it has become public knowledge that we are looking into one particular case of a mutual arrangement made between two newspapers in Canada, and we are aware of the position of the Canadian Press in the sense in which the hon. gentleman refers to it. If any specific case comes to our attention whereby the existence of this agency were used to foster a monopoly by one newspaper or any combination of newspapers, we would, of course, be prepared to investigate.

I have no particular case to refer to, but I wanted to make sure the minister was watching it because in the lakehead community, which in a sense is a

Supply-Justice
unit, we have two newspapers and the owner of one of them has died recently. There was a certain fear expressed on the part of some people, including myself, that the chain which owns the paper in the other town is trying to purchase, and if it should do so it would leave us in that area without any competition at all, which is the cause of some concern. But, of course, we cannot ask the combines branch to take any sort of a priori action.
One of the points I wanted to raise in connection with combines-and the minister will remember that last year I raised the same point that was raised by the hon. member for Skeena today,-was this new policy towards which the department is working, and there are a couple of other points I wanted to deal with also. I want to ask the minister whether he can comment on an article called "Anti-combines and Injury to the Public," written by Mr. George W. Wilson, which reads, in part as follows:
In recent years certain business interests, lawyers, and professional economists have been insisting that the Combines Commission be required to demonstrate more than an "undue lessening of competition" to obtain a conviction under the Combines Investigation Act and the Criminal Code. What is being suggested is that the commission prove that the economic consequences of the anticompetitive business practices complained of are less desirable from the public point of view than they would have been in the absence of such restrictive activities.
Is that one of the points on which the minister and his officials are trying to determine policy, or are they prepared now to say that do not agree with this general criticism put forward?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is too early to give an opinion on that, because we have not formed a conclusion. But that is one of the more significant aspects of the jurisprudence which has been developed as a result of recent cases, and it would be foolish of me to deny that there are various elements in the country which regard that aspect with a great deal of concern. They have brought it to my attention; we have said we will look into it and say whether in our view there is any change to be made in the jurisprudence in that respect.
Can the minister assure us that the policy when it is enunciated will not be based purely on economic considerations, but that political and employment considerations will come into it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, indeed, and I suppose, to be frank, I should admit that no one in my position could make any decision divorced from political considerations-certainly not a provision of that kind.
There is a provision with respect to monopolies and it relates to research into monopolies and their effect upon the economy, is that not so?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is section 42 of the act which authorizes the commission to institute inquiries of its own motion into trade practices generally. Perhaps I should read it. Section 42, subsection 1 of the Combines Investigations Act reads as follows:
42. (1) The director upon his own initiative may and upon direction from the minister or at the instance of the commission shall carry out an inquiry concerning the existence and effect of conditions or practices having relation to any commodity which may be the subject of trade or commerce and which conditions or practices are related to monopolistic situations or restraint of trade, and for the purposes of this act any such inquiry shall be deemed to be an inquiry under section 8.
What is the position of the court, if it gets to the court, with respect to prosecutions and penalties against monopolies themselves as differentiated, if there is a differentiation, from combines?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman means would there be any difference in the position if charges were laid as the result of an investigation started under section 42 or whether they are laid as the result of an investigation commenced in another way. I think if charges were laid then the courts would be in exactly the same position no matter what had been the occasion of the commencement of the investigation. But I should say the purpose of section 42 is rather to conduct the sort of inquiry which might lead to the consideration of recommendations for changes in legislation rather than to laying charges in court.

That is what I had rather expected was the situation, that this was primarily for research purposes and that arising out of it some change in legislative approach might develop with respect to monopolies themselves. I imagine there has been some research along these lines of monopolies and their effect. Could the minister indicate what the results of these inquiries and that research have been with respect to monopolies?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am advised that there are four in process, one in the field of automobile insurance, one in the field of antibiotics, one in the field of discriminatory pricing and the fourth in the field of tires, batteries and accessories. These inquiries are in process. There are two before the commission now, the one relating to discriminatory pricing and the other relating to automobile insurance. These inquiries are

completed as far as the director is concerned and are before the commission for consideration and recommendation. The other two inquiries have not yet been completed by the director. When we receive the report of the commission we will then be in a position to make some further assessments as to whether, and if so what changes in legislation might be indicated as a result of these inquiries.

At the present time, though, apart from what the commission may report, in the minister's opinion at the moment, without taking into account what may be in the report, could he give us any indication what his views are with respect to the legislative program as it would apply to monopolies. Are there any in that field?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think I can give any indication of that. The whole field is being studied and my first responsibility is to make my own conclusions and then draft a set of recommendations and present them to my colleagues in cabinet. Until that is done and until cabinet has accepted, rejected or modified any recommendations that may be made I do not think I am free to hint at what my own views are.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister if there has been any investigation with regard to fixing the price of fish on the Pacific coast. I should like particularly to know what is the present status of any investigation that has been carried on.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, there is such an inquiry and it has been referred to on several occasions in this house. It is well advanced. The taking of evidence has been completed and the evidence is now being compiled so that a statement of the evidence can be laid before the commission.
I am referring particularly to the united fishermen's organization.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. As far as I am aware that is the only inquiry into the field of fish prices that is under way and it was to that inquiry that I had reference in my previous answer.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has one particular case in relation to combines investigations that spills over, as it were, surprisingly enough into the field of agriculture and comes under the purview of the Department of Agriculture.
As the minister probably knows there has been a fairly strong demand in certain parts of the country that there be support prices established for pulpwood. That demand has been especially strong in the maritimes and Quebec and it is present to a degree in
Supply-Justice
eastern and northwestern Ontario. There are a number of difficulties involved in the government establishing a floor price on that commodity. One of the main difficulties is the fact that there is a report concerning the purchase of pulpwood in certain districts in eastern Canada which would dynamite the establishment of any sort of a fair price because, if the information in this document is correct, it would indicate that a fair price has not been paid up until now. This means we are rather chasing our tail in this particular regard. We are not going to get a floor price until we can get something definite in terms of what the floor price should be. We have not had a just market price if the report is correct so how do we get out of the difficulty and arrive at a fair floor price? That is a problem for the Minister of Agriculture but I should like to know what the Minister of Justice could do in speeding up the matter and what are his opinions on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course, as the hon. member himself has said, the question of a floor price for pulpwood is a matter for the Minister of Agriculture. There are, I think, other difficulties in the way in addition to any difficulty that may arise as a result of this report and any prosecutions that may result. There is the fact that in many cases pulpwood is not grown by farmers but is grown by others. How do you in fact set a support price for pulpwood?
In so far as the situation may be affected by this report and action taken thereunder, as I have informed the house the matter has been referred to counsel in the city of Montreal with instructions for prosecution and I can assure my hon. friend that although these cases being complicated, difficult and technical always take a surprisingly long time, nevertheless we do not anticipate any excessive or undue delay in disposing of this matter.

Could the minister say from talking with his commissioner that the combines commission should be in a position to give the Department of Agriculture advice as to what a just market price would have been if it had not been for the restrictive trade set-up that was in operation? In other words, if the Department of Agriculture has to get information and establish a fair price, is the combines investigations commissioner in a position to advice the minister what a fair price might have been?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. I think it would be quite improper for the combines commission or the restrictive trade practices commission to enter into that sort of field at all, but information

Supply-Justice
might be obtained from the report itself and from the facts disclosed there. We are not concerned with the detail of whether this or that particular price was too low or too high. Our responsibility is to assess whether prices have been affected by the activities of the companies concerned on the one hand, and also whether the activities of those companies, or whether there is evidence that the activities of those companies, constitute an offence under the combines legislation. We are not qualified, nor is it any part of our responsibility, to make recommendations as to what the price actually might have been or should be.

Mr. Chairman, one other
matter in connection with combines; I have here a copy of a letter from the general manager of the garage operators' association in Ontario which was sent to the minister on May 29, 1958. The substance of the letter is contained in three paragraphs. These paragraphs read:
The governors and directors of the garage operators' association are greatly concerned by a practice of the oil companies in Ontario which the association's legal advisers have instructed is perhaps both contrary to the combines act and also contrary to the Unfair Competition Act, and in fact and law is likely in restraint of trade.
This practice of the oil companies involves gasoline price wars where prices are reduced by one station serving one type of gas across a community and the gas station attendant is sponsored and recompensed by the gas company and still will go on for some time, one company bettering the offer of another and then suddenly the war comes to an end on the last day and oddly enough the price of gas ends up being the same as it started on the same day for every company in the community and at the same level.
Although for obvious reasons this may be amusing to the oil companies, it is a great injustice to the public and to the small operator.
That is the end of the paragraphs that I feel carry the meat of the complaint. Whenever one raises questions in regard to this he realizes that perhaps he is prodding into areas that would be just as well left un-prodded until some definite action is taken. Since this particular complaint is such a pertinent one right at the present time when gasoline wars are going on in various parts of the province of Ontario,-and I gather also out in Manitoba-can the minister indicate the scope of any possible action in connection with this? Does it look as though it is worth while proceeding on the basis of complaints that have been received so far?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The complaints allege matters which, if substantiated, would warrant investigation with regard to discriminatory pricing contrary to section 412 of the Criminal Code. That was the allegation made by those who brought it to our attention. As a result of

this complaint the director interviewed two of the officials of the associations bringing them to our attention, and he has consulted with them as to the specific nature of the complaint, and the situations complained about are under study in the branch with a view to making a more formal inquiry or investigation as soon as staff is available who are now engaged on other inquiries. Until the inquiry is launched and more specific facts are ascertained we could not give any indication of the direction in which the inquiry may lead us.

What is the staff situation in your department at the present time to handle what may be an increasing amount of business? Have any attempts been made in the past year, let us say, to extend the scope of the activities and has the minister the men to do it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: At the present time the staff is normal in comparison with past years. There are always some vacancies but we are carrying out a competition at the present time with a view to recruiting staff in the category of inquiry officers. If there should be any increase in the numbers of inquiries to be undertaken we shall be in a position to deal with them. The staff has also increased but are fully engaged, particularly the director personally, in the studies and discussion which I have indicated which are taking place with regard to a general review of combines legislation.

I have a question arising out of the minister's last comments with respect to staff. Can he indicate whether there is a backlog of cases to be inquired into and whether he finds when a complaint is raised either by six people or by an order given by the minister, or the director on his own initiative decides to make an inquiry, these things pile up because of a lack of staff members?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am informed there is always some backlog of cases under inquiry at the end of a fiscal year. On March 31, 1958, the close of the last fiscal year, some 30 inquiries were waiting to be proceeded with as against 20, the average of the previous fiscal years. That is one of the reasons why we have conducted this competition for the selection of further junior officers.
How many officers are there?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I believe I said 30 inquiries awaiting attention; a more accurate phrase would be proceeding, as against an average of 20 at the close of previous fiscal years.
How many junior officers were you conducting this competition for?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We would fill up to five
vacancies as a result of the competition.

If my memory serves me right the minister indicated that there were five vacancies in January when this question was last before the house. I think it was January when the estimates were last before the house. There were five vacancies then and there are five vacancies now. Is that the same five? Have they not been filled since that time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am informed that of those five vacancies one has been filled, but another member of the staff has left so we still have five vacancies. The competition was in process last January when I spoke. Civil service competitions do not always get finished as early as one anticipates. But the director tells me that the competition-I am not sure of the technical term-the date for applications has been closed and the civil service commission is in the process of compiling the eligible list now from which the selection will be made.

According to the details on page 244 of the estimates book, 53 employees are listed under the office of investigation and research. In actual fact, that would mean less five, would it? Five of those 53 are potential employees?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, the figures shown here
would be the establishment. Therefore there would presumably be 48 actually on strength at the present time.

I do not know what qualifications you look for in these individuals or what salary structure is offered to them but in view of the qualifications required for such a position, which I appreciate must be fairly high, is the minister of the opinion that the salary structure is sufficient to attract capable people or would more capable people be attracted by higher salaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will notice that the starting salary for combines investigation officers is $5,400 and rises through various grades to $11,000 for combines investigation officers and $12,500 for senior combines investigation officers. I am informed that the salary ranges compare reasonably with the rest of the public service in similar categories of skill and qualifications and that our experience in recruiting staff at these salaries is about the same as other departments.

I am going to suggest that
in all probability the staff is far too small and that if it were larger the branch, merely by being larger, would be in a better position
Supply-Justice
to conduct many more inquiries than are being conducted at the moment. I am sure the minister will probably agree there are many conditions existing across the country involving organizations on a nationwide basis or smaller groups in provinces or municipalities that require investigation because these organizations are in fact operating contrary to the provisions of the act. If a larger number of people were employed on the staff to investigate these cases there would be a far more beneficial effect on the economy and the general public than there is at present.
I am going to make a suggestion arising particularly from what the hon. member for Port Arthur said with respect to gasoline price wars. I have also heard comments from four or five individuals in cities across Canada that price fixing arrangements are entered into between gasoline retailers in those cities similar to the situation which existed in Vancouver a few years ago but that no action is taken to deal with them. It may well be the reason is that the matter has not been brought to the attention of the director in one way or another. In any event, if these conditions were brought to his attention and if all the other illegal practices being followed which have not come to his attention were brought to his attention the present staff would be even less able to cope with such cases than it is at the present time. I suggest that there should be an ample increase in the numbers of the staff in order to police the provisions of the act properly.
Extensive amendments were made to the act in 1952 and I suggest that since then individual corporations, feeling that it is beneficial to their business from a profit point of view to operate combines for fixing prices or to restrict distribution, markets, warehousing or anything else in order to ensure control of a certain market and the highest possible income, are finding ways and means of escaping the eye of the director. In past years it has been indicated in reports of the commission that one way in which evidence of illegal combinations came to light was through extracts from correspondence between companies with respect to how they were going to carve up markets and fix prices. However, in order to overcome that they are writing fewer letters and there are more telephone conversations with respect to price fixing and other illegal acts. Therefore it will become more difficult to ferret out and discover evidence leading to the establishment of the operation of a combine, which is what is required if we are going to be able to cope with the problem.

Supply-Justice
Even though the minister may not now have any clear idea of what changes will be made in the legislation, and I hope he will not be too long in making up his mind about necessary changes, I hope that he will indicate now that there will be an increase in the staff for the administration and policing of the Combines Investigation Act in order to ensure that under our society the interests of the public will be served.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think I should let those remarks go without comment. Possibly the hon. gentleman might be interested in this general statement of the activities of the branch as at the end of the fiscal year, March 31. Sixteen new inquiries were commenced during the 1957-58 fiscal year. The number of formal investigations of possible contravention in progress at the end of the year was 30 compared with 20 in progress at the end of the previous fiscal year. The number of general inquiries in progress was 4 against 3 at the end of the previous fiscal year. Four prosecutions were successfully concluded during the fiscal year and one prosecution was commenced. The total combined staff of the restrictive trade practices commission and the director of investigation and research was 51 at the end of the 1957-58 fiscal year compared with 50 at the end of the previous fiscal year. The staff of the director included 16 investigation officers compared with 15 at the end of the previous fiscal year. There is also the competition to which I have referred which will result in an increase of anything up to five. This would be an increase of 33J per cent in the investigational staff in the office of the director which would, of course, be a very substantial increase.
Therefore I do not think there is real justification for the comments made by the hon. member. With respect to the existence of the fact to which he refers, namely that companies are finding ways and means of escaping the eye of the director, I can assure him that this is far from the case. If he sat at my desk he would know about the benevolent but watchful or should I say watchful but benevolent eye that the director keeps on the activities of these companies and he would know of the feeling of business in Canada that the director is a man who is remarkably able to exercise the supervision which it is his responsibility to exercise under the legislation under which he is appointed. Therefore I do not think the hon. member need have too much fear on that score.
I am sure the minister was not trying to construe my remarks as casting any reflection upon the director.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. I took the hon. member as saying that he questioned whether the director had an adequate staff to carry out his responsibilities. I can assure him that the experience of those concerned is that with comparatively small staff they do an enormous volume of work and exercise a very remarkable degree of surveillance over the field for which they are responsible.

The only remark I wanted to make in connection with salaries is this. It seems to me that if most of these officers are going to have legal training there might be a special adjustment in the salary scale. I know the House of Commons has a great many lawyers in it. I know that here they get $10,000 a year approximately. Yet I understand from talking to almost all of them that this is a tremendous come-down. If we assume that lawyers in the House of Commons are average lawyers, it would appear that the wages paid to investigation officers are rather poor for people with that particular training.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend will appreciate that while the starting salary as reported in the blue book of estimates is $5,400, the next grade up is $7,500 and the next one is $8,300, the next $10,000 and so on. These, as they start, would be lawyers, economists and accountants who would normally be quite recent graduates from their respective professional schools. It therefore is not a case of our trying to get men who are earning large amounts in their profession and getting them to come in at small salaries. We recruit them as fairly recent graduates and then train them through the department with the increase in salaries shown here.

My only comment is this. The fact that members start and finish at $10,000, unless they are lucky enough to become parliamentary assistants, may be the unfair part. On June 10 the minister is credited with having said in Vancouver in a speech to the retail merchants of Canada that his department is carrying out investigations into two fields, an inquiry into loss leader selling of cigarettes, electrical appliances, hardware and jewellery trade and a study of whether some types of grocery stores receive unfair price preference from the supplier; it is reported that in this address the minister said that steps are being taken to remove "artificial" obstacles to small business in Canada. This general or rather-I must be fair-slight indication of what was the meat of the minister's argument on this particular occasion I am sure would interest all of us at the present time.

As the minister is aware, across Canada- and usually out of a local marketing situation-small merchandisers are wrought up over the fact that, for example, the big chain is able to offer cigarettes so much more cheaply. The appeal of the small retailer and the small merchant is a very powerful one, as the minister himself has remarked. What is his general thinking with regard to the way in which this particular problem can be attacked by the combines investigation branch? With the number of officers that was mentioned that they had, surely it is apparent that they cannot attack this problem on a continental scale; that their way of attacking it has to be based upon picking some specific market and trying to use that as an example right across the country. I wonder just how effective that approach would be. Perhaps that is not the approach that the minister had in mind when he announced this matter. I would appreciate hearing his comments in regard to this problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
To mention some of the inquiries that have been instituted, inquiries into cigarettes or practices with regard to cigarettes have been instituted both in Edmonton and Toronto and also Ottawa and Hamilton; and with regard to electrical appliances in Vancouver. With regard to discriminatory prices in the grocery trade, that inquiry is a general inquiry which will take in the whole of the country.
With regard to the availability of staff to carry out these inquiries, as I have pointed out there are 30 formal investigations of possible contraventions and 4 general inquiries under way at the present time. As to what the restrictive trade practices branch might do to help small business, of course the completion of these studies will give us an indication of what should be done. If in fact it is shown that the section regarding unfair trade practices is not an adequate protection then we will know whether we require additional legislation. I might say that the most universally expressed desire of small businessmen in so far as matters in our field is concerned is for the repeal of section 34. These men say that they have lost the protection against the big chains which the resale price maintenance system formerly gave them. They say that they are now at the mercy of unfair selling practices, loss leader practices and so on. It is to give us a fresh starting point or a starting point to assess what action we can take in this department that will be helpful that these inquiries are under way.
My remarks at Vancouver referred also to the proposal made by the government to set up a small business section within the administrative machinery of government to which
Supply-Justice
these men might bring their problems. Ours is only one of the aspects of the problems with which small business is faced in the field for which this department is responsible.

The minister by his comments indicates that he is aware that there is a paradox in this whole problem of small business. The position of small businessmen and the sort of rat trap they have got themselves into appeals to us because we like the idea of the small businessman having an opportunity, especially in the line of competition. Yet to save the small businessmen in a sense we have to wipe out the advantages that very large organizations are able to obtain through competitive means. I wonder whether the minister can express an opinion or his views on whether, if the small businessmen or the small merchants are given the kind of legislation that will enable them to get away from this unfair advantage that they feel the big companies have, we will be getting ourselves into the situation where we are actually denying the whole essence of the legislation itself which is to encourage competition.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think I must say that the hon. gentleman has put his finger on the very problem that we have to wrestle with. I do not know that I can do much more than put the matter in that way. It is certainly the policy of this government, as I understand it, to encourage the maximum degree or the maximum number of independent enterprises. The traditional way of putting the matter is, of course, whether you want to see the small independent corner grocery maintained or whether you want to see people served by a chain store. To reconcile the steps which may be required to be taken to protect the small independent operator on the one hand with the desire to maintain the maximum of competition on the other hand is the problem with which we are faced. That is one of the thorny problems towards which this study is directed. It is not an easy one to solve. That is why I make no forecast as to when I will be in a position to make a recommendation beyond saying what I have said, namely that we hope we can resolve our thinking on this and other aspects of the matter in time to make recommendations for next session.

I should like to leave this question by making these two points. I had a conversation the other day with a gentleman who told me several years ago about a combine that was operating in the fine papers business. As the minister knows, proceedings were taken. There was an investigation followed by some prosecutions. The information

Supply-Justice
he gave me was that so far as he was concerned, and he is in the specialty field dealing with retailers and wholesalers of paper, the combine is just as strong as ever despite what may have taken place. I asked him to give me this information in printed form with signatures so that I could use it. He refused because he said he was thinking of his own protection. I just wanted to make that point. This gentleman felt that this particular situation still exists despite the activities of the combines branch and the prosecutions that have been undertaken.
I believe I mentioned this other point last year. It has been brought to my attention again by a man in the automobile business who refused to put his name to a sheet of paper because he is involved with one of the big automobile manufacturers. He insists that there is a system of kickbacks arranged so far as the financing of automobiles is concerned, depending on the volume of business done. In other words a man who is selling cars and who has a very large volume of business is able to arrange for certain kickbacks with the acceptance corporations at the beginning of a year's financial operations which give him a much better margin on which to work in selling the cars on credit than the smaller dealer is able to obtain.
As I say, I asked this man to put these facts on paper but he said if he did he would just get himself into trouble since most of the people about whom he would be complaining were in the business with some of the acceptance corporations and some of the large automobile companies. I should like the minister to have his commissioner take an interest in this problem, if possible, to ascertain if there is any substance to this charge.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. gentleman we will be very glad to do that. I can assure him also that if any person feels a reluctance to reveal his name or put the matter in writing, if he calls at the office of the director he may be seen personally and the interview will be entirely confidential. It may well be that if information is given which results in a prosecution, at that stage witnesses might have to come forward. Certainly, however, in the preliminary stages, until we get the matter advanced to the point where a decision as to further action has to be taken, an interview can be entirely confidential.
Indeed I see no reason why the name of an informant should not be confidential throughout until it becomes a matter of gathering evidence. As I said a few moments ago, it would seem to me that the gathering of that type of evidence would not involve revealing

the name of the person who first gave the lead to the inquiry. I think it would be safe for me to assure my hon. friend that he can tell his informant that if he cares to come to the office of the director of research and investigation there can be a discussion there that can be kept confidential.

Last year I had an interview with the director, and he was kind enough to give me some advice in connection with pulp-wood prices. As you know, if you can get six people to request an inquiry it has to proceed. I was supremely confident that I could get six people. I landed home in my constituency and went canvassing, but I have to be quite frank and say I was only able to get two names, although I could get dozens of people who would agree with the general complaint. It is for this reason I know that particular section of the act does not work too well in initiating investigations. I am hopeful that the commissioner will not hesitate at all to act on his own initiative in following these leads. We welcome the assurances that have been given that the minister gives his whole-hearted support to these activities.
May I ask one other question? The other day the minister, in response to a question of mine, indicated that Mr. Meighen in the city of Winnipeg-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Brandon.

-in the city of Brandon, had been retained to study the evidence relating to the acquisition of Manitoba Sugar Company by B.C. Sugar Company, and to proceed with a prosecution if he felt there was sufficient evidence. Could the minister indicate what the position is with respect to that matter at the moment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The counsel named is studying the evidence. He was instructed on July 10 and we have not had a report from him as yet. It is a little early to expect one.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
165. Office of investigation and research, $446,321.

I should like to ask the Minister of Justice if the director of investigation and research, under the Combines Investigation Act, either independently or through the royal commission on patents, has made any recent study to ascertain whether the Canadian patent system has been used by the holders of Canadian patents in a manner that might be considered to be detrimental to industrial growth in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am informed that the office has not made any study of patents, as a general study of inquiry. Patents do come up

incidentally in connection with our cases and are then dealt with on an ad hoc basis.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Penitentiaries-
167. Administration of the office of the commissioner of penitentiaries, including $60,000 for grants to recognized prisoners' aid societies, as may be approved by the treasury board, $518,701.
I should like to ask the Minister of Justice-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit me to interrupt a moment? We allowed item 158 to stand, remission services. Before we go on to penitentiaries, may we either revert to that or carry it as part of the department itself?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall 158 carry?
Agreed.

On 167 again, then, may I say that I realize the present minister has only been in this post since June of last year. I am wondering whether or not it is possible now for him to give a review of his study of the penitentiary situation since he has taken office, and what he has in mind for the future with reference to that type of institution. I know that we will have before us in a few days a motion for second reading of the parole bill, so I am not going to discuss that phase of penitentiaries. Only a few days ago the minister announced that he hopes, within a period of the next two months, to have a meeting between his departmental officials and the attorneys general of the provinces concerning the major sections of the Fauteux report. Even although these announcements have been made by the minister, could he give us a little more information as to just what he has in mind with regard to the penitentiary system itself, and the inmates who have to be in these institutions. I have not visited all the penitentiaries in Canada, but I have been through some.
For how long?

O.k., smart boy, as an M.P., I got in and got out. I hope I always will be able to get out. I hope the Minister of Justice will not mind if I draw to his attention the fact that penitentiary buildings in Canada are hopelessly outdated and antiquated. One has only to visit them to know that.
So my first question to the Minister of Justice is this, and I address it to the minister through you, Mr. Chairman: how can you, as Minister of Justice, believing, as I am sure you do, in modern penology, in particular from the point of view of rehabilitation, hope to achieve any success with
Supply-Justice
completely outdated and antiquated institutions? And we have as yet had no pronouncement of any policy of change with respect to the capital structure of the penitentiaries themselves.
Go to Kingston, and visit that institution. I am not questioning the work of the warden, his deputy or his officers. I think they are trying to do a wonderful job. But how can they do the job they are expected to do? How can you, as Minister of Justice, obtain the results you hope you can obtain by a new approach when you have an institution so antiquated and outdated? I hope the minister can give us at least some indication as to his thoughts along this line with respect to the modernization of these penal institutions so that they may coincide with modern penology and its thinking on the subjects of supervision, treatment and rehabilitation.
Further, when we think of penitentiaries- and this is not a nice subject-we have to study those who are in these institutions, and I was disappointed when I read the report of the commissioner of penitentiaries for the period ending March 31, 1957 to note that 12.94 per cent of the population represented people under 21 years of age and that of the 703 persons who were under 21 years of age at that time only 232 were in prison for the first time. Thus, of those in the penitentiaries in the year under review the majority even of those under 21 years of age were recidivists. That should make us ask ourselves whether our penitentiary system is working out satisfactorily with respect to these young people.
At the same time as I studied the report of the commissioner of penitentiaries I read for the same period, the report of the warden of the Okalla jail in British Columbia which deals with the same subject. I note that the warden says in his report at page BB9:
The increase was made up partly from the growing numbers of teenagers who, for lack of adequate alternatives to delinquency, and a deficiency of preventative services in the community, are not being dealt with in time to avoid the inevitability of sending them to prison.
And in this report-I am speaking now of the report of Warden Christie, who, I think, is outstanding in the field of penology in Canada-it is pointed out that there is a need for facilities for those awaiting trial, for proper segregation and for psychiatric treatment and psychological advice.
I should like to return now to the report of the commissioner of penitentiaries in which it is pointed out that 12.94 per cent of the prison population were under 21, and of the 703 people represented by that percentage approximately 400 were recidivists. I know how deeply the minister feels about this

Supply-Justice
problem; I know he has a bill on parole coming before us, and I know he is arranging this meeting in two months time with the attorneys general and his officials, but in view of the seriousness of the situation and in view of the outmoded capital structure of our penitentiaries I wonder whether the minister could give us an indication of his views and of the progress of his investigation and, possibly, his hopes and aspirations as to what may be achieved in the not too distant future.
Before the minister replies, I wonder whether he could also say what the situation is with respect to Newfoundland where I believe there is not, in fact, a penitentiary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think I should explain at the very beginning with regard to what I must say in reply to the hon. member for Vancouver East that I must sound a note of caution, since any program I outline, tentative though it may be, is not one which I could say would be fulfilled in the near future.
I think we are confronted with a major task here in bringing the penal system into line with the best thinking as to what a panel system should be. An enormous amount of capital expenditure must be made if the plans which we are developing now are to come to fruition. I think that for this reason, as well as for the reason that it is going to take time to train staff and that we may well have to assume responsibility for a very substantial increase in the population, both the physical and the financial implications of this program may well dictate that it be carried out in stages, perhaps three separate stages of, maybe, five years each.
Perhaps I should deal at this point with some of the things which are now being done. The hon. member has stated that our penitentiaries are antiquated as buildings. Perhaps they are not quite as antiquated as that bald statement, accepted without modification, might indicate, because I am informed there has been a substantial rebuilding program over the past number of years in the institutions themselves, quite apart from any new building program. In Kingston, for instance, to mention one example, three shop buildings have been completely rebuilt since 1954. And, to speak of new institutions, a new federal training centre was opened at St. Vincent de Paul in 1952. That is a completely new building, as well as a new departure.
Is that Collin's Bay?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, that is the federal training centre at St. Vincent de Paul in Montreal. The new institution at Joyceville

was started last year in 1957. Its construction is well on now. We have a small number of people there and hope it will be ready for full occupancy in the summer of next year.
In addition there is a completely new building-it will almost be an institution in effect-to be started again at St. Vincent de Paul the authority for which is given in the supplementary estimates this year. An appropriation of $800,000 is being asked for to start the building of that new institution at St. Vincent de Paul.
There is at the present time a substantial building program both recently completed and in progress but we recognize that this building program has been designed and is designed to take care only of the present penitentiary population and to some extent the anticipated increase in penitentiary population under the present division of responsibilities between ourselves and the provinces. We recognize, therefore, that this new building program is designed only to take care of that portion of the penitentiary population for which we are responsible now and even then we know we shall soon have to be starting new buildings in addition to those I have mentioned just to take care of our own responsibilities. It becomes obvious then that if and when we accept responsibility by agreement with the provinces for a very considerable increase in the number of prison inmates, namely all those sentenced to terms of over six months, our capital requirements for building are going to be vastly increased. It is a question of whether we can meet that problem in part at least by taking over some of the provincial institutions in which these men are now accommodated or whether we are going to find we have to provide entirely new buildings for them and until, therefore, our discussions with the provinces are completed we will not know the full extent of our building requirements in this field although we are aware, as I say, that in order to meet the expansion of our own present responsibilities, owing to increased population and so on, we are still going to have to continue with a building program.
What are the sort of things then that we have in mind as other measures of reform? I have said we are fully conscious of the need for new buildings and new types of buildings and our problem is the contemplation of the implementation of that program although, as I say, it is going to have to be stretched out over a period of years. Therefore, what we have to do is design a program.
What about some of the non-physical aspects of our thinking? There are such

matters as the training of staff in connection with the line of thinking we are now following with regard to parole, for instance, which is designed to return as quickly as it is possible to do so the maximum number of prisoners to lead a useful life in society outside the walls of a prison rather than inside. In order to make that program workable and realistic and to ensure that it serves the best interests of society we are going to have to have considerable increases in trained staff so the parole system will be an advantage rather than a disadvantage. That is a matter involving both physical as well as financial outlays as well as administrative problems in recruiting and training staff and problems of consultation with the various institutions, universities and so on where a good deal of the initial training, schooling or education of that type of staff should take place. Schools of social work will be involved.
Then there is the question of the type of facilities which will be provided. There are the recommendations of the Fauteux commission in this respect, of course, as to segregation of types of offenders. That, of course, if carried out increases the number of institutions that may be required and so it involves both an administrative as well as a financial problem. Then there is the other important recommendation for reception centres where prisoners might be classified before they are committed to the final institution in order that they may be sent to the right type of institution where the right type of rehabilitation training designed to suit the needs of that prisoner would be available. In a country as wide as Canada it might be impossible to have only one reception centre. We may have to have more than one and I believe the ideal objective would be a number of reception centres adjacent to the pentientiaries so that the transportation costs and delays might be cut down. The reception centres in turn would require classification staffs, men or women trained in the assessment of prisoners, in assessing their need and the type of rehabilitation they require so they may be properly assigned to the proper institution when the proper institution is available.
I say these things in order to indicate the line of our thinking. We are attempting to develop a scientific and socially adequate system of penology in Canada, one designed to serve the best interests of society and designed to keep our prison population to a minimum -that is, the population inside the prison walls-and to ensure that men committed to prison receive the type of consideration, education, handling and rehabilitation training that they need and which is designed
Supply-Justice
to return them as quickly as possible as useful members of society rather than as continuing enemies of society.
I would conclude this summary of the sort of program we have in mind by saying it must be realized it is going to be an expensive one in terms of dollars. I doubt very much- and I think this warning should be sounded and sounded now-if we are going to be able to point to savings in terms of dollars. Our population is growing. Probably the numbers coming into prison for the first time will continue to increase. What we want to cut down on is on the number coming back to prison. This is indeed going to be an expensive program and, as I say, we probably will not be able to point to savings in terms of dollars. But I believe that when it is established on the basis we envisage we shall be able to point with pride in Canada to the fact that we have brought our system up to date and to the fact that we are achieving substantial savings in terms of social and sociological results.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are a number of considerations which I think indicate or argue in favour of confining the person under sentence of death to jail in the province. In addition, there would be the occasion of the last visits from relatives and friends of the sentenced person. I think all of these considerations argue in favour of the retention of that man in jail close to-his home.

I should like to ask the

'lr. Speaker.]
does the department use its own architects, or does it engage the services of architects of the Department of Public Works, or does it invite independent architects to do the drafting and make suggestions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In connection with penitentiaries generally, the policy is that because they are specialized institutions they require a specialized type of construction and so on, and we have therefore developed within our own department, and within the penitentiaries branch a specialized staff of architects and engineers for this purpose. With respect, therefore, to the preparation of plans for the design of institutions, our own staff exclusively are engaged on this work, and we do not retain the services of outside architects or engineers. However, with respect to some special projects-I could mention the sewage disposal plant at Joyeeville as one example -which are to some extent not of a peculiarly penitentiary aspect, we do, I think, retain the services of outside consultants with regard to the preparation of the plans.

I can understand that the designing of a penitentiary may be best done by men who have specialized in that work, but with regard to the discharge of plans and specifications, specifications particularly, I should think that is within the scope of work of the architects employed in the Department of Public Works and that their services might be utilized in the interest of economy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think if the hon. member
were to ask the Minister of Public Works, he would be told that the staff of his department is fully engaged on the department's present construction supervision and engineering projects. We have, as I say, developed a specialized staff within the department and it would therefore seem to me, at least at present, to be a duplication if, having prepared the plans and being familiar with their requirements and specifications, we should then turn the work over to another department for supervision and construction when our own staff is qualified to do this work.

I should like to ask the minister a question with reference to Alberta. As the minister knows, a person who is convicted in Alberta is sent to the Saskatchewan penitentiary at Prince Albert. In my early days in Calgary, I got to know something about the jail situation in that city, and I said some years ago, and I think it bears repeating, that if John Howard were to walk in and see the jail situation in the city of Calgary he would be just as shocked as he was at conditions 200 years ago, because they only have 19 beds and on many occasions they have 50 customers. Some arrangement should be worked out between the federal government and the province with regard to a penitentiary. I might also mention that Drum-heller is in the Bow River constituency, but the chamber of commerce is most anxious that if there is going to be a penitentiary built in Alberta it should be just outside of Drumheller.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand the question to be this: have there been discussions between my department, or the penitentiaries branch and the government of Alberta with regard to the construction of a penitentiary in that province. I think the answer must be that I have discussed this matter informally with the deputy attorney general of Alberta whom I met shortly after I was appointed Minister of Justice. I discussed with him some of our problems in connection with penitentiary construction and some of the problems arising out of the Fauteux report. The deputy attorney general indicated to me that they themselves had certain plans in contemplation for the construction of provincial jails, and said that it would be helpful if we could give an indication of whether or not we were prepared to accept the Fauteux committee recommendations regarding this government accepting responsibility for provincial sentences to terms of over six months, since this would help them to finalize their plans. I explained the difficulties we had in making a final decision, some of which I have referred to earlier, such as the physical and financial obligations we should have to assume if we accepted such a responsibility, and I explained our general plan of making a study in our own department after which we would communicate with provincial attorneys general and call a conference.
I know that the government of Alberta, together with governments of other provinces, is anxious to have this conference. We have now arranged for it to take place some time in the month of September of this year. But apart from this informal and personal discussion I am informed there has been no correspondence between this government and the government of Alberta on the subject.

Mr. Chairman, with your indulgence and that of the committee I should like to first pose a problem and then suggest a remedy. In my riding in British Columbia there is a small city called Fernie.

During the past year this city has been hard hit by the closure of the coal mines in that area. Fernie was a one-industry town. We are now seeking a means to bring back the stabilization of the economy of Fernie. One means by which this could be accomplished would be through the establishment there of a penitentiary. There are several points in connection with the establishing of a penitentiary in or near the city of Fernie which I should like to bring to the attention of the hon. minister.
The city of Fernie is an ideal location for a penitentiary. We have two roads, one east-bound and one westbound in the same location. Air, rail and bus transportation facilities are available. Not far from the bus transportation there is a plot of land consisting of 1,600 acres which could be available for the construction of a good-sized penitentiary in the area. I would respectfully request the hon. minister to give full consideration to the possibility of locating a penitentiary in this area.
It has been brought to my attention that there is a tendency on the part of the Department of Justice to centralize penitentiaries across the province. Hon. members will agree that many of the larger industrial concerns in Canada have found that it does not pay to centralize too many departments or plants in one area. I suggest that decentralization of penitentiaries should be taken under consideration by the hon. minister and his department.
I have heard it stated that a problem exists with respect to a lack of opportunities for the rehabilitation of prisoners after they have left a penitentiary. In the city of Fernie and in the Kootenay East area opportunities are available for the rehabilitation of released prisoners. I have been advised that the residents of the lower mainland of British Columbia do not wish to have a penitentiary constructed in that area. There is in Fernie a considerable amount of arable land which is potentially good farm land available in my area for the construction of a penitentiary. In several places the available land would amount to several hundreds of acres.
Although the city of Fernie would be close at hand to the site of any penitentiary that might be constructed in the area and would provide attractive homes for the employees of the institution there would be no danger of the city encroaching on the penitentiary area as has happened in many other areas where penitentiaries have been constructed. The city of Fernie offers every facility offered by a well-established community. It has a golf course, an ice skating rink with artificial ice, and has available ice curling

Supply-Justice
on artificial ice, swimming facilities, skiing facilities complete with tow rope and offers opportunities for hunting, fishing and other sports.
Is that part of the penitentiary area?

The establishment in
Fernie of a penitentiary would have the effect of bringing people into the area and providing the personnel of the penitentiary with an attractive community in which to reside. We have a modern gymnasium with badminton facilities, churches of all denominations, modern schools, a modern hospital and medical centre, a good library, theatres and closed circuit television. The establishment of a penitentiary in this area would also help to revitalize and stabilize the economy of the city of Fernie which has been damaged as a result of the closure of the mines and it would have an equally beneficial effect throughout the Kootenay East area. The proposal for the establishment of an institution in this area has been supported by the chamber of commerce, the service clubs and various organizations throughout the province of British Columbia.
. This morning I attended a meeting of the committee on external affairs where I observed that we were prepared to spend over $35 million under the Colombo plan. May I say to the minister that charity begins at home. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that I appreciate what has been said by the hon. member for Kootenay East and to assure him that I am well aware of the interest of the city of Fernie and the district surrounding it in the establishment of a penitentiary there. I wish to assure the committee that the hon. member for Kootenay East has been most assiduous and has left no stone unturned in bringing to my attention the desire of those in that area for such an establishment and the reasons which occurred to them why it would be a suitable area for the location of a penitentiary.
I have discussed the matter with the hon. member personally and, as he knows, I have had correspondence from the mayor of that community which I have also discussed with him. I can tell the hon. member now, not

having had an opportunity to do so before this, that earlier this morning I was in telephone communication with the chairman of the industrial development committee of the Fernie board of trade. The interest of the area in such an establishment there is well known to myself and to the officials of the department and particularly those of the penitentiaries branch.
I have tried to be as frank in the matter as I can. Knowing the economic situation in that area I felt it would be grossly unfair to hold out any hope or expectation which might not be possible of fulfilment. I have therefore had to explain some of the considerations which would have to be taken into account in determining where a penitentiary will be located. There are, of course, two aspects to this problem. The one is related to the establishment of a new penitentiary under our present responsibility in which case certain considerations would have to be borne in mind which I have communicated to the hon. member, particularly with respect to the desirability of having reasonably available and adjacent to such an institution the facilities for a rehabilitation training program. I have also pointed out that with respect to any new building program which may be dependent upon an agreement with the provinces for the assumption of the extra responsibility referred to in the Fauteux commission report, namely the assumption by us of responsibility for those receiving a sentence of more than six months, there may be some different types of institutions to be built or provided by the federal government. I assured them that with respect to both the extension of the existing and present penitentiary building program and the construction of new types of institutions which might be made necessary after the provincial conference and as a result of any agreement arrived at we will bear in mind to the fullest extent the interest of the Fernie area and I can repeat that assurance here.
However, I do not think it would be fair for me to go beyond that assurance because until we know just what it is we are going to have to provide we ourselves will not be able to determine what building program we will have to undertake and therefore it would not be sensible for me to indulge in speculation now as to what locality we will select to establish any new institution.
In addition, of course, I must in fairness to all the other municipalities and areas interested point out that ever since it has been indicated that we are eventually going to embark on the construction of new institutions in western Canada some 100 or more municipalities or areas have pressed upon the

department the peculiar suitability of their area for such an institution.
We will have to survey the whole available field and, in fairness, I think 1 must say that when we make a decision it will have to be made in accordance with what seems to be the best program of building that we can devise.
I close, however, by assuring the hon. gentleman that in making that decision we will bear the interests and the facilities of his area fully in mind.
