Mr. Chairman, I do not want to delay unduly the passing of the estimates of the Department of Justice, but I should like to take advantage of this opportunity this evening to congratulate the Minister of Justice who, I know, is laying the groundwork of some kind of strategy for a more effective struggle against obscene literature by those who are responsible for public morality and order. I know that the minister realizes the seriousness of the problem and that he is prepared to solve it. It is more than ever urgent that some effective legislation be enacted as soon as possible. Let us hope that the following steps will be taken:
1.	Include in section 150 of the criminal code a "practical" definition of the word "obscene";
2.	Amend the criminal code to make it possible to serve a summons, as is now done in Great Britain, upon the newsdealer or bookseller who has been found in possession of publications considered obscene, so that he might put forward his objections, if any, to a court order for the destruction of the said publications;
3.	Prevent publishers from making "package" deals that is to say from forcing newsdealers or booksellers to take "all or nothing", as is currently done at the present time;
4.	Extend the charges under the act to the publishers of obscene literature.
As long as the above-mentioned steps are not taken, groups now campaigning against obscene literature will be hampered in their activity. I realize the difficulties of the problem. It is a matter of getting rid of obscene publications without interfering with the freedom of the press. This calls for a precise definition of the words "obscenity" and "freedom".
At the present time, our courts base their interpretation of "obscenity" upon a judgment rendered in 1868 by a British court and according to which "the criterion of obscenity consists in deciding whether the matter charged as obscene tends to deprave or corrupt those whose minds are open to such immoral influences and in whose hands such a publication might fall." That definition is not so bad. It would be a matter of deciding whether a publication is such as to cause moral prejudice. Mr. Raoul Mercier, crown

attorney for the county of Carleton has used that definition with some success already.
Nevertheless I will go along with the Minister of Justice when he states that it could well be more "practical". Personally, I would prefer a provision which would prohibit publication and distribution of any or all literature whose chief characteristic is the exploitation of one or several of the following subjects: sex, crime, immorality, horror, cruelty and violence.
With regard to the freedom of the press, it should be remembered that liberty is not synonymous with licence. The press is not "free" to corrupt and deprave morals, even under the guise of "information". That is the basic principle upon which the minister should guide himself if he wishes to amend the criminal code.
I would most heartily approve of any of the above amendments, especially those aimed at prohibiting "block sales" or "package deals". There are publishers now who require a dealer to buy objectionable publications if he wishes to buy the others. That is an intolerable practice. It is really deplorable that a certain number of publishers and newsmen should attempt to make money by the exploitation of the basest instincts of their readers. Some specialize in detailed description of crime. They plunge their readers in the blood of the victims and in the dark inner recesses of the murderer's heart. Others exploit sex for all it is worth. Finally, there is a third class of objectionable and nefarious publications. I have reference here to those committed to the spreading of rumours, to scandal-mongering, and muck-raking. They fling mud right and left, and especially up.
Most professions have boards which impose proper ethical standards upon their members. There should be such a disciplinary body among newspapermen, who could assume on their own behalf the defence of the genuine freedom of the press by the elimination of corrupting undertakings that are a menace to this fundamental social freedom.
How are we to deal with the widespread circulation of this large number of objectionable publications which corrupt the minds and hearts of our people?
1.	Amend the criminal code;
2.	Encourage people to refuse to buy filthy publications;
3.	Promote good reading by urging educators to encourage appreciation of good literature by young people.
Finally, I ask the hon. Minister of Justice to amend the Criminal Code as soon as possible so as to do away with unwholesome publications. It is urgent. Obscene literature is to

a great extent responsible for juvenile delinquency which is a burden for the state and costs huge sums to governments. A tide of juvenile delinquency is sweeping over our cities. It is the most accute problem of our age, next to atomic weapons.
I urge promoters of all morality campaigns to keep up their good work.
In the diocese of Joliette, there is, as at L'Assomption, a committee against bad literature. I congratulate these people and encourage them to continue their struggle in co-operation with municipal associations and authorities. I would be very happy if the hon. minister could in the near future, amend, if possible, the Criminal Code in that sense.

Mr. Chairman, allow me to say a few words in support of the remarks just made by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), about obscene literature.
I have no doubt that the minister has trouble finding ways to eradicate that cancer that has crept into our literature. I therefore believe that we should give him our support in his effort to find, as soon as possible, an appropriate definition of obscene literature either through an amendment to the criminal code of by some other way, so that our people might be saved from that scourge.

Mr. Chairman, for over forty years the Kootenay country has suffered from lawlessness and various forms of violence which in recent days have been extended to the Okanagan. This matter is of most serious concern to the people residing in the interior of British Columbia, possibly of more concern than ever before in our history and, of course, of serious concern to all in Canada who are concerned with this social problem. In past years we have suffered the burning of schools, the burning of houses, the bombing of railroads, the bombing of power lines on repeated occasions, recently the bombing of a bus station and the bombing of a good number of other sites throughout the Kootenay district.

The latest apparent evidence of the continuance of this lawlessness is the number of forest fires lately which are considered by the forestry branch of the province of British Columbia as having been caused by persons who set them deliberately. Anyone who has lived in our district knows what it means in a dry period such as the last two months to fear the starting of forest fires by arson. So the situation is very serious indeed and in some respects tense.
I have refrained so far this session from making any comments on the matter because I was of the opinion that while discussions were going on between the representatives of the government of Canada and representatives of the government of British Columbia no good purpose would be served because this is far too serious a matter for anyone to attempt to make political capital out of it or take any political advantage. I was hopeful that the minister's visit to British Columbia, his discussions with certain persons there and his later correspondence with the premier of the province would result in some co-operation between the federal and provincial governments to formulate a program to deal with the problem in a constructive way not only in the immediate future but in the days farther ahead.
I am not underestimating the difficulty. Before proceeding, may I say that I have discussed the matter personally with the minister on a number of occasions and I am fully aware of his keen interest, his great concern and his willingness to co-operate with the province of British Columbia and with other persons who want to do something to remedy a situation that has existed for so many years. However, Mr. Chairman, time is flying. It is now some weeks since discussions first commenced and I understand that the government of British Columbia made representations to the federal government for assistance in this matter. Apparently no program has been established to date as the result of co-operation between the two governments and so violence and lawlessness continue.
You can well understand the attitude of the residents of the district, municipal officials and other authorities. They are becoming increasingly concerned about what appears to be the failure to design a constructive program as a result of federal-provincial cooperation, and I am of the opinion that it is going to take close co-operation between the federal and provincial governments as a result of agreement to meet this very serious situation effectively. The situation is such that the people of the district I have the honour to represent are demanding that

concrete evidence be given that there will soon be an adequate program to meet it.
I am not going to take the time to go into all the details. speechtext: I might point out that the hon. gentleman is so hard up for subject matter with which to delay the house he had to go back ten years, to 1948.
To 1954; that is not so long ago.

I am glad to have this opportunity, Mr. Chairman, to put forward for the consideration of the Minister of Justice, within whose jurisdiction these matters come, a few suggestions that would involve amendments to the Criminal Code-
Would the hon. member speak up? We cannot hear him.

-to the Canada Evidence Act and to some other related federal statutes. I have no doubt that at the next session of parliament the Minister of Justice will be bringing forward some amendments to these statutes and I should like to think he would bear in mind the suggestions I am about to make, with a view perhaps to including these among any amendments he might then propose to introduce. I do not boast of any particular qualifications to discuss these matters other than the experience I have had in the process of law over a number of years, and particularly my connection as counsel for the defence in a number of criminal cases.
Arising out of that experience I think I have had an opportunity to see something of the need for the changes I am about to suggest to the minister and which I hope he will bear in mind. I want to speak very briefly first about our habitual offender legislation. With reference to the legislation now applicable to habitual offenders, section 660 of our Criminal

Code which provides for their preventive detention classifies a person as being a habitual criminal if:
(a)	he has previously, since attaining the age of eighteen years, on at least three separate and independent occasions been convicted of an indictable offence for which he was liable to imprisonment for five years or more and is leading persistently a criminal life, or
(b)	he has been previously sentenced to preventive detention.
The experiment with preventive detention for habitual criminals began in this country in 1947 and we, therefore, have the benefit of 11 years' experience with its operation. It had been recommended in 1938 by the royal commission on the penal system of Canada known as the Archambault commission.
The habitual offender in Canada is not treated very much differently from the ordinary penitentiary inmate and is not housed in a separate institution. The total number of persons presently undergoing preventive detention in Canada as habitual criminals is 53. The distribution of these individuals among provinces is as follows: British Columbia, 13; Alberta, 5; Saskatchewan, 5; Manitoba, 10; Quebec, 2; Ontario, 13; New Brunswick, 1; Nova Scotia, 4; Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, none. The majority of individuals now undergoing preventive detention as habitual criminals were convicted of offences against the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act-in British Columbia, 7; Alberta, 4; Manitoba, 9; Ontario, 11 and Quebec, 1-making a total of 32.
Our Criminal Code provides for a review by the Minister of Justice of each case every three years, the idea being to determine whether or not the person undergoing preventive detention should be permitted to be at large on licence. It is open to the minister to conclude that he should not be released and it is, therefore, quite possible that such an individual would spend the rest of his life in prison.
Once an individual has been found to be an habitual criminal he is permanently removed from the jurisdiction of the courts. He has no right to be represented by counsel at the time of these periodic three-year reviews by the minister. The minister is not required to give any reasons for his refusal to grant a licence and there is no appeal from his judgment. If a man is released he can be rearrested and taken back into custody without resort to the courts or without the protection of a public trial. As I have already pointed out, the number of persons proceeded against as habitual criminals and found to be such since 1947 is 53.
It goes without saying that large numbers of individuals now at large and never proceeded against under this provision of the Criminal 57071-3-203
Supp ly-J ustice
Code could properly be found to be habitual criminals. The main reason why proceedings are not initiated against such persons is the perfectly understandable reticence of the majority of permanent crown officials to invoke proceedings the effect of which could be to doom a man to a possible lifetime in penitentiary. This is a reticence with which I have every sympathy and I do not wish to be taken as meaning that wholesale prosecution under this legislation should be instituted against everyone now at large who could be found guilty.
However, the fact remains that the legislation in its application has been inexcusably discriminatory. Only 53 persons have been selected out of a much larger number to be proceeded against in this way, to be removed forever from the jurisdiction of the court, to become subject to the whims and fancies of particular police officers, crown officials and others. All this strikes me as being alien' to some of the most ancient and sacred principles of our criminal law.
When this legislation was first introduced into parliament the then minister of justice, Mr. Ilsley, was far from being positive about it, for at page 4685, column 2 of Hansard for that year, he said:
While legislation of this kind was recommended by the Archambault commission, the government has no wish to be dogmatic about the necessity for it, and while recommending it, is prepared to give careful consideration to any views which may be expressed by members of the house regarding it.
It is interesting to read the contributions to the debate at that time of some of the hon. members of the house. I think that our experience over the last 11 years confirms the apprehensions that were voiced by some of them at that time. For example, the present Prime Minister, had this to say as recorded at page 5058 of Hansard for 1947:
Criminal law being what it is, it should be uniformly enforced in all parts of the dominion without regard to the wishes of individual attorneys general. In this section there is a marked departure from the uniformity which should be aimed at. This section means that for the first time in the history of our criminal law there will be a departure from uniformity of application in all parts of the dominion.
And further on, the present Prime Minister said in the same context:
I urge upon the minister that this introduces into our criminal law a lack of uniformity, in that a person in one province may be prosecuted as a habitual criminal, whereas if the same person committed a crime in another province he would not be subject to prosecution.
The hon. member for Cartier at that time, Mr. Hartt, put it rather aptly in my opinion when he said:
I am wondering whether we are not committing a crime against criminals.

Supply-Justice
It strikes me now in the light of our long experience with the law that the objections of the various members of that day were well taken and they showed a foresight which the subsequent administration of the law has tended to confirm.
There has been a complete and utter lack of uniformity in the application of the law. The frequency of prosecution has varied from province to province. Specially appointed federal prosecutors in cases under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act have been far more prone to resort to the use of this legislation than have the ordinary crown attorneys of the various judicial districts. When one considers the crushing effect of an indeterminate sentence and stops to realize to what extent a man's freedom for the rest of his life is subject to the whims and fancies of a few police and prosecution officials, and when you further consider that the Criminal Code already provides adequate penalties for all of the offences contained in the Code, it seems to me that it is now time to consider that the experiment with this legislation has been a failure and that it should be abolished.
Dealing with the right of crown counsel to cross-examine a prisoner on his previous criminal record, the practice today as prescribed in section 12 of the Canada Evidence Act, permits crown counsel to cross-examine any witness-including an accused person who gives evidence on his own behalf-about any previous conviction for a criminal offence.
There is no limitation whatever on this right. When an accused person is tried by jury the law imposes upon the trial judge an obligation to caution the jurors where evidence of the criminal record of the accused has been adduced in cross-examination, that such evidence is relevant only to the credibility of the accused witness, and he must also admonish them against using it as evidence that he is the sort of person who would be likely to commit the offence for which he is on trial.
Speaking from a long experience I think I can safely say that the prejudice created by disclosure of a criminal record is overwhelming, and no amount of caution by the trial judge in conformity with the rule I have mentioned is adequate to disabuse the jury's mind of its harmful effects.
The prospect of being cross-examined on a criminal record has dissuaded many accused persons from giving evidence and in my opinion over the years large numbers of accused men have been convicted either because of the prejudice resulting from a disclosure of their criminal record or from their failure
to testify by reason of it. They might, if neither of these factors had existed, have been acquitted.
I recall so well in personal experience the case of an accused person whose criminal record consisted of eight previous convictions for serious offences. On the occasion on which I was acting in his defence he was charged with the murder of his brother. The account he gave to me of the circumstances, which was to some considerable extent confirmed by two other witnesses, ordinarily would have furnished him with a good defence of self-defence. If such a defence were to have prevailed he would have been acquitted but because of his criminal record it was unsafe for him to testify in his own defence because of the prejudicial effect that disclosure of his record on cross-examination would have had. A conviction for murder might well have been the result. He was duly convicted of manslaughter and notwithstanding the jury's recommendation for extreme leniency the trial judge imposed a sentence of fifteen years imprisonment.
I am in the fortunate position of being able to say that the recommendation that I am now putting forward received the unanimous endorsation of the Canadian bar association at its annual meeting held in Ottawa in September 1955. In that connection the bar association urged that section 12 of the Canada Evidence Act be amended so that as amended it would provide that while the right of cross-examination on the record of a person charged and called as a witness would not be abolished it would be greatly curtailed. For example, it could be brought out that a previous conviction had been registered against the accused witness if proof of that conviction were relevant to prove the guilt of the offence with which he was charged; and also if he personally or by his advocate asked questions of the witnesses for the prosecution with a view to establishing his own good character; or if he gave evidence of his own good character; or if the nature of the conduct of the defence were such as to involve imputations on the character of the prosecutor or the witnesses for the prosecution; or if he gave evidence at the same trial against any other person charged with the same offence; or if he had previously been convicted of perjury. The bar association recommended that this unlimited right as it now exists which I submit is an unfair right should be curtailed.
It will be observed that this change does not and is not intended to interefere with the present practice of proving the criminal record after a conviction has been registered for the purpose of assisting the magistrate

or judge to determine the appropriate sentence. It is my belief that this change is long overdue.
The next change for which I feel a serious need exists arises out of section 624 subsection 2(b) of the Criminal Code. This section reads as follows:
The time during which a convicted person
(a)	is at large on bail, or
(b)	is confined in a prison or other place of confinement pending the determination of an appeal by that person, does not count as part of any term of imprisonment imposed pursuant to his conviction, but paragraph (b) is subject to any directions that the court appealed to may give.
As you can see from the provisions of the section I have just read, where a convicted offender exercises his right to appeal his conviction, no part of the time that it takes to bring the appeal on for argument counts as part of his sentence in the event his appeal is unsuccessful unless a special order directing that it should count is made by the provincial court of appeal.
I can recall in Ontario that up until about eight years ago invariably the court of appeal, which had dismissed the appeal of a convicted offender, would direct that the time served in custody pending the appeal should count. It was only very, very rarely that such an order was refused. We grew to expect it as a matter of course. Then an abrupt change in this practice occurred for reasons that were really never made very clear and the exact reverse became the rule. Since then, in the great majority of cases where an appeal is unsuccessful the court will refuse to direct that the time served should count and the prisoner's sentence therefore does not commence to run until the date upon which the appeal has been disposed of.
. This certainly has had the effect-a highly undesirable effect in my opinion-of reducing to a very exceptional degree the number of criminal appeals brought before the court of appeal. The fear that there may be delay in prosecuting his appeal and that his appeal might fail has tended to dissuade many a convicted offender from going to the court of appeal to have his conviction and the trial proceedings that lead up to it reviewed.
I have often felt that if a practical method Could be worked out every conviction-certainly for a major crime-should be reviewed by an appellate court. I cannot help but think that if the conviction of everyone serving a sentence in our Canadian penal institutions were today reviewed the result would be to flush out of prison large numbers of inmates either by virtue of some irregularity at trial or for some other reason. In saying this I do not wish to be taken as meaning that our 57071-3-203i
Supply-Justice
prisons are filled with innocent persons. The point I am trying to make is that, in my opinion, there are many persons serving sentences as a result of trials which an appellate court would, on review, find had not been conducted according to law.
Delay in proceeding with an appeal is not ordinarily the fault of the accused man. The delay is usually occasioned by the delay in receiving from the court reporter the transcript of the notes of evidence taken at the trial. It will often be the fault of the counsel for the defence and sometimes the fault of counsel for the crown, and on occasions-especially when judgment is reserved for a lengthy period of time-the fault of the court of appeal itself. It does not seem right that a prisoner should be penalized by reason of a delay for which he was not responsible.
The present law works a hardship also in the case of convicted offenders who are unable to furnish bail pending the hearing of an appeal. In the case of a first offender whose crime has not been one of violence, or of exceptional gravity, it is usually possible to secure his release on bail. He suffers therefore no hardship by the present operation of the law, but the first offender, who is poor and is unable to furnish bail, is thereby discriminated against. As one who believes that the court should constantly be developing, applying and interpreting our law, I find a good deal of difficulty in accepting a policy such as the one that now prevails which in its application discourages appeals. I strongly urge, therefore, that the Criminal Code be amended so as to provide that time served in custody, pending the hearing of the appeal, should count as part of the sentence as a matter of course.
Finally, I would like to say a word in respect to minimum sentences. There are certain offences in respect to which the magistrate or judge has no discretion. He must impose a minimum mandatory penalty. For example, theft of anything from the post after it is deposited in the post office and before delivery is an offence under section 298 of the Criminal Code for which a term of imprisonment of not less than six months must be imposed. So also in the case of second and third convictions for driving while one's ability is impaired or for drunk driving and so also in the case of offences under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, and indeed for a number of offences under other federal statutes as well.
We all read in the Toronto press some months ago of the case of a young woman charged with theft from the post-theft of an ordinary letter-as a result of which she netted nothing except a few pennies and

Supply-Justice
the magistrate was reluctantly required to impose the minimum penalty of six months in a case in which it was apparent he felt suspended sentence would have been the proper dispositon. It is true she was quickly released on ticket-of-leave but all others are not so lucky.
In cases under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, any person in possession of a drug must be sentenced to a minimum mandatory period of imprisonment of at least six months. I have personally witnessed the application of this provision in the case of a helpless drug addict for whom suspended sentence and treatment would have been the answer. It was the case of a gentleman who, with the assistance of his wife, had over a period of about two years by the most enormous exertions of his will succeeded in overcoming his drug addiction. As a result of an altercation in which he had become involved he was rendered unconscious and brought to a hospital, whose authorities of course were unaware of the history of drug addiction and drugs were administered to him to ease the pain and in consequence the former appetite which he had succeeded in overcoming was revived. After a period of about six months he was arrested and charged with illegal possession of narcotics. Medical evidence that was called at his trial, where he pleaded guilty, established that he was capable of cure and that he had been responsive to treatment and that he should be permitted to continue this treatment. I can still recall-notwithstanding the eloquent efforts of crown counsel to obtain the severest possible penalty-how much anxiety the trial judge felt when he imposed that minimum sentence of six months. His personal desire was to place the accused man on suspended sentence and probation to enable the course of treatment to be followed but his hands were tied by a law which, in my respectful opinion, was and is iniquitous.
When they receive their appointments our judges and our magistrates are deemed to have common sense and good judgment and, in my opinion, they should be given the power to use this judgment unfettered by statutory rules concerning minimum sentences. I would ask the minister, Mr. Chairman, to bear in mind the suggestions I have just made. Thank you.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think that the remarks of so eminent and qualified an authority as the hon. member for Park-dale should be allowed to go unanswered or without an expression of appreciation and tribute. Very few members of this house are better qualified by background, experience or aptitude to speak on the subjects to

which the hon. member has just addressed himself and I assure him that I personally and the officials of my department both appreciate and will study closely the suggestions he has made.
With respect to two of them, I think I can dispose of the matter quite shortly by saying that we are fully prepared to-and to some extent may almost have anticipated the desire of the hon. gentleman-have those matters looked at.
With respect to habitual criminals, we are certainly prepared to admit the necessity and the desirability of having a look at the provisions to see what, if any, modifications should be made in those provisions.
With regard to the right to cross-examine an accused on his criminal record, the same thing applies. We are prepared to have a look at this, to study this in the light particularly of the recommendations of the Canadian bar association. It is my impression, based on recollection only, that at the present time the matter is before the commissioners on uniformity of the law, criminal section, for study.
With regard to the matter of time spent in confinement pending the hearing of an appeal, the hon. gentleman certainly makes a very powerful argument, although I am not quite certain I would accept every aspect of the case he has made. However, I respect his great knowledge of the subject, particularly in so far as appeals are concerned.
The man is in jail.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, I know that, but I may say that not all aspects of the argument made by the hon. member should be accepted. I am not prepared to debate them at this time because, as I said, the hon. member has made a very powerful case and one which we are going to look into.
With regard to the question of minimum penalties, here again there is perhaps some room for difference of opinion and the difference of opinion can be maintained or retained with respect for the opposite point of view. There are, however, I believe only three sections of the Criminal Code which provide for minimum penalties at the present time although there are, it is true, other federal statutes which have minimum penalty provisions. I do point out to the hon. gentleman that if there is a clear example of a case where the minimum penalty results in a sentence which is in excess of that which is appropriate under the circumstances, then the provisions of the Ticket of Leave Act, administered by my colleague the Solicitor General, do afford in general a ready remedy for that situation and, as was the case of the

woman recently convicted in connection with theft from the mails, that course was followed and there was an almost immediate exercise of the prerogative under the Ticket of Leave Act. The reason I make this point with regard to minimum sentences is that I think there is a good deal to be said for the requirement of minimum sentences in some cases in order that necessary measures of rehabilitation, reform and training may be instituted.
I admit that those sentences could perhaps be left to the discretion of the court and if it appeared to the court that the circumstances of the particular offender necessitated or justified a longer sentence in order that reform or rehabilitation methods could be instituted, then the court should adjust the sentence accordingly. But, under the present state of the law and of the training of staff and in the absence of a system-we have to admit its absence-of pre-sentence reports; in the absence of a scientific and complete system of pre-sentence reports so that one can be certain that every aspect regarding the circumstances of the convicted man are drawn to the attention of the trial judge there is, I submit, an argument in certain cases for minimum sentences and justifiable, I think, only on the basis I have suggested, namely that it may be necessary in some cases in order to permit of necessary reform and rehabilitation training to be instituted.
But having said that, I still admit to the powerful argument made by my hon. friend. I do not say this to detract from his argument and I assure him that this matter also can and will be looked into in connection with the study which it is anticipated we shall have with the attorneys general arising out of the recommendation of the Fauteux committee with respect to this matter of the bringing about of uniformity in the sentencing practices of the court. This is one of the matters up for study. Therefore, it may well be found that once the uniform practice and the pre-sentence report system have been developed, this argument I have made in connection with minimum sentences will no longer be adequate. If that can be done, then I think it would be better to leave it to the discretion of the court. That whole matter will be studied and developed at the forthcoming conference.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the outset may I take this opportunity on behalf of myself and my colleagues to offer my best wishes to the Secretary of State on his birthday. I know the position he is in this evening, this being the first time he has presented estimates to the House of Commons. I wish him well in his office, as I have done before on other occasions. This is the first opportunity I have had to say how relieved we were that in the recent accident in which he was involved he came off without injury and we hope that his very charming wife is having a rapid and happy recovery.
There is one thing that is unfortunate so far as discussion of these estimates is concerned. I refer to the fact that we do not have the reports of the different departments administered by the Secretary of State. They have not been printed and that makes our position a little difficult in questioning the minister if we have to take each item and ask for comparative figures corresponding to the report we have on hand, that up to March 31, 1957. Knowing that these reports are not at hand I trust that the minister will supply as much information as possible from his own records and will not have to be requested for details on each item from this side of the house.
The Secretary of State administers a great number of departments including, of course, one of the most important, the civil service commission. I hope that his tenure of administration will be long enough so that he may acquaint himself with the problems of the civil service and the commission. After all, the government of Canada is a very large employer and depends upon its employees to carry out the various functions of government. I hope that the minister will always consider himself the champion of his employees and be willing to answer at all times on behalf of the employees of the government. If at any time some hon. members feel inclined to deride or criticize some of the employees in the civil service, who have no opportunity to defend themselves, I hope he will rise in his place, ask for particulars and defend those who are responsible to him and the government.
I also hope that he will take great interest in the revision of the Civil Service Act. We have heard very little about the revision of the act but I understand from press reports and statements made by civil service commission officials that a study of the act has been going on for some time, something which is long overdue. Of course, the Civil Service Act was drafted many years ago at a time

Supply-Secretary of State when the relationship between the employees and the government and the number of employees were much different from today. I think the system has been established now that the appointment of servants of the crown should be done on a fair basis, should be done by examination, by merit, that promotions should be by merit and that all relationships between employer and employees should be the best and above the standard existing in ordinary industrial and commercial enterprises.
I think we all have reason to be proud of our civil service. I have said before, and I am sure all members agree, that the civil service of Canada is the best in the world. Our civil servants are efficient, loyal and as hard working as any other group of employees in commercial undertakings anywhere. If there is any fault involving a small number of employees it is just as negligible as in any other big business.
The problems, as I have outlined before, are mainly those relating to promotion, wages, appeals and working conditions. I hope that in drafting the new act the powers of the commission will be properly defined. In my opinion it is not clear in the minds of members of the house exactly what are the powers of the members of the civil service commission. There is always a doubt that there is some other power exercising a greater authority than the civil service commission in important matters relating to employees of the crown. Of course, I know that treasury board has to have that control which is necessary in approving expenditure and that the size of wage increases has to be subject to approval by the cabinet. But in any event I think the new act should make clear what are the powers of the civil service commission in selecting and promoting employees, hearing appeals from employees and suggesting wage scales. Once that has been established I think the government should insist that all matters within the powers of the civil service commission should be decided by the commission and that employees should have the right to appeal to the commission and be heard before a proper board with respect to any matters on which the commission grants leave to appeal.
I am not at all satisfied that at present the right of appeal with respect to promotion is satisfactory. I hope that the system will be revised. I am not satisfied either that when civil servants are dismissed with or without cause a proper appeal is provided that is satisfactory to both parties. I have had a great deal of experience in this city with civil servants and I must say, having in mind the rights granted to members of unions working in commercial establishments, that
[Mr. Richard (Ottawa East) .1
our civil servants have been very reasonable and I think they should be granted more privileges under any new act than they have been granted in the past.
I also think that the civil service commission should have the right to make more effective recommendations as to working conditions. Those of us who have lived in or around Ottawa for some time know that our establishments are not the most suitable and that, for example, objections involving ventilation, light, heat and cold are made with regard to almost all the buildings where civil servants work. I do not give credit to any former administration for having done any better but I hope that in the future the civil service commission will have the right to have a voice with respect to the new buildings which will be constructed for the government, and will have a say as to the type of equipment, ventilation, light, the size of offices et cetera so that our civil service will have working conditions which are suitable and, as I would hope, the best of any.
Sometime ago we heard that a study would be made with respect to wage increases in the civil service. I understand that at this time the civil service commission has completed its study and has transmitted it to the cabinet. I cannot hope that the minister will tell me that the wage rate has been set or that the wage increase has been granted or refused; however, I would hope that he could tell me that the civil service commission has completed its study and that it is now up to the government to decide whether any wage increases are to be granted or whether the matter is to be studied further.
(Translation):
And now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words to the Secretary of State about bilingualism. It is incumbent upon him in his new functions to see that bilingualism is respected in government documents and publications. It is also incumbent upon him to see to it that the civil service commission requires respect for bilingualism in appointments when such is required.
I should particularly like to remind him that a French-speaking candidate should not be called upon to fill only a position where the knowledge of French is required if, in addition, he can speak English. Not only should he be eligible for any position offered by the civil service commission but he should be given some preference in view of the fact that he speaks both languages fluently. The minister has expressed his opinion on this matter in the past and, now that he is a member of the cabinet, I hope that he will bring

the same attention to this problem and protect the interests of those candidates.
It is not my intention at this moment to go fully into the other branches of the Secretary of State Department. However, I should like to know if the minister will report to us on the commission under the Inquiries Act, to inquire into the working of the Patent Act, the Copyright Act, the Industrial Designs Act, and other related legislation, as well as on the trade mark service.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, at the outset, may I say to the Secretary of State (Mr. Courtemanche) that we are happy that though he is celebrating his birthday today this does not appear to have aged him in the least. We wish him very many happy returns of the day.

No, even though he is an extremely genial gentleman that we all like to meet. I would also like to extend to his wife my best wishes for a prompt recovery.
I have no intention of detaining the house for any length of time nor to create trouble for the Secretary of State in any way. He is a most genial gentleman, that we all appreciate. I was happy at his appointment and I know that this is the first time he is bringing down his departmental estimates, something which is always difficult and somewhat unpleasant. I hope that he will not get into that habit for too long before he is replaced and that he will make good use, on this side of the house, of the experience he has acquired where he is sitting now.
As the member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard) said a moment ago, a very important feature of our life here in Canada is our civil service. Our civil service is made up of highly competent persons, appointed after examinations designed to determine their fitness for the particular job concerned, and with no political interference. I know that at this time there is some uneasiness within the ranks of civil servants. This uneasiness has been brought about by certain members who, having made some rather inconsiderate promises, have been attacking civil servants and accusing them of meddling in politics. These people are in a most uncomfortable position at this time. As far as the great majority of them
Supply-Secretary of State are concerned, they certainly do not deserve to be called by the names they have been called.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I cannot speak as beautiful French as he does, but I am better aware than he will ever be of the civil service problem, and with his dull wit, his lack of serious learning, he will never be able-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Back home we call these people "smart Alecs".

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Yes, "smart Alecs", but I know some of those "smart Alecs" which are much cleverer than that one.
I was speaking about the civil service, a matter which the hon. member for Roberval cannot grasp, because of his dull wit. I was saying that some members-and perhaps he is one of them, but I am not accusing him of being one of those who could do such things-have aroused some ill-feeling in the ranks of the civil service. I believe the Secretary of State should give some assurance to civil servants that they will not be molested without at least being given the opportunity to defend themselves. If the civil servants are guilty of meddling in politics or of any other activity inconsistent with their duties, I think they should be punished as anyone else, but I believe they are also entitled to be heard and to have their case defended.
I feel that the charges which were levelled against a federal civil servant without his being afforded an opportunity to defend himself constituted an act of dishonesty on the part of the person who preferred those charges. I feel that the Secretary of State, who is a serious and able person, should take the bull by the horns and act in this matter, even if cabinet colleagues of his be the ones who abuse their power to crush certain civil servants. He should say to them: "At least, if you have any charges to make against a civil servant, you will do so in such a manner that he will have an opportunity to defend himself, to be fairly tried, as any other person should be fairly tried". The Secretary of State knows this is no exaggeration. I suggest he do what is required so that such people may be heard and may, if necessary, have some one take up their defence.
I have no intention of detaining the house too long, but I wish to talk of another department which comes under the Secretary of State, the printing bureau.

Supply-Secretary of State
I said a moment ago that there was uneasiness in the civil service and I now say that there is also uneasiness in the printing bureau and that is due to the fact that one man, believing that ministers go but that he stays on, behaves in a high-handed way with the staff. I am referring to the queen's printer.
It is high time this man learned that even the humblest of his employees is entitled to some consideration. I have received several complaints from civil servants whose names I will not mention, for fear of reprisals. The employees are dissatisfied, but are afraid to say it openly, and I think the Secretary of State would act creditably in launching an impartial inquiry, where people could speak freely, knowing that their statements would not be repeated to the czar of that department, and I feel sure that this inquiry would uncover startling things.
I am even convinced that the Secretary of State has never been informed by the queen's printer of the many complaints made about the cafeteria. Yet, he was made aware of many complaints, which have remained in his files. Indeed, I believe that some doctors have said that the food there was unfit for consumption and that, if the employees want to stay alive, they should go and eat somewhere else.
I believe that an investigation should be made about that situation. It would be very important that such an inquiry be carried out in such a way that the complainants would not be identified. I always fear for them, since there are many ways of dismissing an employee, and if their names were known, they might not be dismissed for what they have said but some way would be found of laying them off later on for some insignificant slip. I would therefore suggest that the Secretary of State make this inquiry so that an understanding may be reached.
I know the Secretary of State means well and that he will consider the case of those employees with sympathy. If an employer or high official heading a department- because the employer is always the State- does not always act as he should towards his employees, he should be put in his place and told of his duties and responsibilities towards people under him.

I should like to make a few remarks on the same general subject as that dealt with by the two gentlemen who have preceded me. I have always abhorred the wording for the classification "civil servants". I do not care for the title. I think it is rather a degrading way of making reference to those people who work in the service of Canada. I rather hoped that we could find

some other classification or category for the people in the public service. However, inasmuch as there is no other category perhaps in my remarks I shall have to make reference to the people in the public service in an effort to avoid the use of the phrase which I do not care to use. I do not believe this phrase adds much to the stature of the individuals, those people collectively, who work in the public service of Canada in so far as their relationship with their employer, in this instance the crown or the government of Canada.
I hold the same ideas in this respect that I have held for quite a number of years and which were expressed in my own province with respect to the same group of people who work for the provincial government. We in the C.C.F. are somewhat of the same opinion as the hon. member for Ottawa East, who spoke earlier, in so far as the relationship of these people with their employer is concerned. We believe a channel should be provided, somewhat similar to that which exists for other groups of employees, by means of which grievances in connection with working conditions may be settled. Employees working for private companies, and for some crown companies in this nation, are provided with means whereby these grievances may be settled. Employees in the public service who have grievances arising out of what they may consider to be improper cause for discharge, questions of wages, hours and working conditions, should not have to adopt a cap in hand attitude to their employers. They should not have to say, please, we would like to have an adjustment in wages, or we think it is necessary for these reasons, or we would like to have a change in our working conditions, and these are our arguments for them. They should not have to say, we think that such an individual or group has been dealt with incorrectly and we think some redress should be given to them. These employees should not have to go on bended knee, as it were, and I am not being critical of the attitude of the government in this respect but merely of the relationship between employees and the crown or the government itself.
These people in the public service should be treated in the same manner as other groups of employees who come under federal labour jurisdiction. They should have the right, as some have now, not only to organize into unions representative of their type of work, but they should have the right to apply for and receive a certificate of bargaining authority. They should be in the same position in approaching their employers with respect to negotiation as are the employees of the Canadian National Railways, which is a publicly-owned corporation. They should be able to

sit down, within a certain time limit, and bargain with their employer, in this case the federal government, in connection with all matters which they consider to be subjects for negotiations.
On the other side, the government would be in precisely the same position of being able to negotiate with representatives of these employees with respect to matters that the federal government felt needed changing. May I call it ten o'clock?

1.	Are United States forces in Canada governed by the NATO status of forces agreement?

4.	Were any members of the United States forces charged in the civil courts of Canada in 1956 and 1957? If so, how many?
Answer by: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of
National Defence):
1. Yes.
2 and 3.
